To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the brain is a massively distributed system; and (b) the brain is massively parallel.
the human brain is a complex system of interacting parts and that these parts change in response to changes in the environment.
(1) the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is a critical site for visual recognition memory, and (2) the hippocampus and related medial temporal structures are not necessary for visual recognition memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the mind and brain, and with how the two are related.
understanding the brain as the organ of mind.
how information is processed by the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neuroimaging is a tool for answering certain types of questions, but that the questions themselves are not determined by the tool.
we do not yet know enough to answer many of these questions. But we do have the tools to begin to answer them, and it is the task of cognitive neuroscientists to do so.

we have a long way to go before neuroimaging can provide a comprehensive account of the brain's implementation of cognitive processes, but that we can make progress on many of the questions that are of interest to us by using neuroimaging to answer specific questions about the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is an organ that is capable of supporting the mind, and that the mind is a process that is supported by the brain.
the human brain is a complex and flexible information-processing device.
the brain is not a computer. It is not a computer because computers are designed to do one thing at a time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the end, neuroimaging is not a substitute for good behavioural science; rather, neuroimaging can help us ask better questions and design better behavioural studies.
neuroimaging can provide a powerful tool for understanding the mind-brain relation, but only if it is used in a principled way to address specific questions.
neuroimaging can be a very useful tool for studying the brain, but only if we have good questions to ask and a clear understanding of the strengths and limitations of the methods we use.
